newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarians rush for dollars as lev tumbles.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarians rush for dollars as lev tumbles.

text.p: Bulgarians rushed to convert their savings into dollars on Friday as the local currency reached new all-time lows, saying they had lost all confidence both in the lev and in the banking system.
The International Monetary Fund last week proposed introducing a currency board to stabilise the economy by curbing inflation and restoring confidence in the lev.

"They are saying that a currency board is a good thing for our country. Maybe they are right but it will take months to introduce and I have to take care of my money today," said Svetla Gospodinova, 29, buying dollars at an exchange bureau in central Sofia.

The head of the State Savings Bank, Bistra Dimitrova, told parliament on Friday two billion levs had been withdrawn from her bank since Monday and some clients were asking the bank to buy back their Treasury paper ahead of maturity because they feared it would not be redeemed in cash.

The State Savings Bank is Bulgaria's largest savings institution. Other commercial banks said they had not seen a run on deposits yet but did not rule out big withdrawals if the lev kept falling at the same rate.
Central bank intervention brought the lev back from lows of 284 to 275 at the close.

"One thing is for sure, I'm not going to keep my money in a bank," said businessman Roumen Angelov, 36. "With the currency board in place, the central bank will stop pouring money into the commercial banks and they will all go bankrupt so the safest is dollars in cash at home."
The central bank is seeking bankruptcy through the courts for 13 illiquid banks. Officials have warned more could close if a currency board curbs central bank refinancing operations.

Under the currency board scheme, the amount of levs in circulation must be exactly matched by the central bank's hard currency reserves. They have been used by Argentina, Estonia and Lithuania to restore confidence and help defeat hyperinflation.
Bulgarians face a tough winter. Annual inflation is put at 240 percent but energy prices, which went up again on Thursday, have risen 326 percent for the first 10 months of 1996.

President Zhelyu Zhelev met ambassadors of the Group of Seven wealthy industrialised countries and Russia on Friday to seek their political and financial support and suggested Bulgaria should seek a debt rescheduling from the Paris Club of government creditors.

"Setting up a currency board does not mean just voting a law and passing a package of measures, it means parallel implementation of structural reform and privatisation, which needs more funds," Zhelev told reporters.
Prime Minister Zhan Videnov supports the proposal, which must be approved by parliament.
Central bank governor Lyubomir Filipov told parliament Bulgaria would not be able both to service its foreign debt and to introduce a currency board without external support.

"We can cover the levs in circulation and commercial banks' minimum reserves held at the central bank with the current foreign exchange reserves plus the gold," he said. "Then, however, there will be no money left to cover debt payments."

Payments of $300 million on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt fall due in the first quarter of 1997. Central Bank foreign exchange reserves stood at $541 million at the end of October, compared to $1.43 billion in October 1995.

One bright spot was news of the sale of a 60 percent stake in Sodi Devnya, Bulgaria's largest and most profitable chemical complex, to U.S. firm General Chemical Group Inc for $160 million, providing cash badly needed to get the country over the next few weeks. Bulgarian Brady bonds rose on the news.
